detail:

BofA raised its BP price target to 535 GBp from 525 GBp but maintained an 'Underperform' rating, citing limited upside to Q4 consensus estimates.

According to Koyfin data, 11 out of 19 analysts covering the stock rate it 'Buy' or 'Strong Buy', while seven rate it 'Hold'.

Separately, Stonepeak completed its acquisition of a 65% stake in Castrol, with BP retaining a 35% interest and CPP Investments participating as an indirect minority holder.

BP PLC (BP) shares drew investor attention on Monday after multiple analysts raised their price targets following the oil major's third-quarter results.

According to The Fly, BofA raised its price target to 535 GBp from 525 GBp while maintaining an 'Underperform' rating. The firm said BP's third-quarter results exceeded the strong indications provided in its trading updates, but sees limited upside to consensus estimates for the fourth quarter.

BofA also expects the company's upcoming Capital Markets Day to prioritize continued balance-sheet repair and portfolio changes before share buybacks resume in 2028.

BP shares traded 4.2% lower at the time of writing.

Analysts Update BP Price Targets

RBC Capital raised its price target on BP to 720 GBp from 700 GBp and keeps an 'Outperform' rating on the shares, The Fly reported .

Similarly, JPMorgan also raised its price target on BP to 720 GBp from 700 GBp and maintained an 'Overweight' rating on the shares, according to The Fly.

Yesterday, Wells Fargo raised its price target on BP to $63 from $57 and maintained an 'Overweight' rating. The firm said that even if the third quarter marked peak conditions, BP's liability repayments were being pulled forward, leaving "headroom for shareholder returns" in 2027, according to The Fly.

According to Koyfin data, 11 out of 19 analysts covering the stock rate it 'Buy' or 'Strong Buy', whereas seven rate it 'Hold'.

Stonepeak Completes Acquisition Of 65% Stake In Castrol From BP

Separately, Stonepeak announced Monday that it had completed its acquisition of a 65% stake in Castrol from BP, which will retain a 35% minority interest in the lubricants business. Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) is also investing in the transaction as an indirect minority holder.

The new ownership structure is intended to give Castrol greater financial and operational flexibility to accelerate growth across its existing markets and adjacent sectors. The company supplies lubricants and thermal management fluids to consumer automotive, commercial and industrial customers.

JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), Bank of America (NYSE: BAC), and Citigroup (NYSE: C) are putting billions behind their share buyback programs, with each bank authorizing at least $30 billion in repurchases.

All three banks released third-quarter results in mid-October, offering updates on their finances and their future plans. Which ones have actually followed through on these share repurchase agreements, shrinking their share count and giving investors more bang for their investment buck?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
JPMorgan has the biggest buyback but the slowest pace

In June 2026, JPMorgan's board authorized a new $50 billion common stock repurchase program, effective July 1. And during the third quarter, JPMorgan repurchased around $1 billion in common stock but recorded only $664 million in net repurchases. In other words, that gross amount used only about 2% of the new authorization.

And not surprisingly, the impact on the share count was modest. The company ended September with 2.656 billion common shares outstanding, compared with 2.722 billion a year earlier. That means its share count declined just 2.4% year over year.

There's a reason for the slower pace.

Management has emphasized that repurchases must compete with other uses of capital, including investments in the business, lending opportunities, and the maintenance of a strong balance sheet. The bank also faces risks around weaker credit quality and investment banking activity.

On top of that, at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 13 times, its valuation also leaves less room for disappointment than its peers'.

A faster $40 billion buyback is shrinking Bank of America's share count

Bank of America has had a $40 billion common stock repurchase authorization in place since Aug. 1, 2025. By June 30, 2026, the bank had around $17 billion remaining under the authorization after repurchasing $13.2 billion in the first half of the year. Then, during the third quarter, it repurchased another $6 billion of common stock.

That brings the program's total repurchases to $29 billion, leaving $11 billion available. Put differently, it has used roughly 73% of the authorization in about 14 months and at its current pace, that remaining amount could be used relatively quickly.

title: Gen Z Lags on Key Life Milestones but Leads in Retirement Saving, Early Investing
detail:
Gen Z Lags on Key Life Milestones but Leads in Retirement Saving, Early Investing
Elizabeth Guevara
Sun, November 1, 2026 at 7:30 AM MST 3 min read
BAC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Gen Z is falling behind on many financial milestones, besides investing in the stock market and for retirement.
Credit: Getty Images
KEY TAKEAWAYS

Generation Zers have a spending-to-savings ratio that's higher than that of older generations.

Gen Z is also delaying major milestones like homeownership and having children due to rising costs and slower wage growth.

However, Gen Zers are investing in the stock market and saving for retirement earlier than previous generations.

Young adults may be more inclined to buy themselves a "little treat," even at the cost of savings. But they're investing for the future earlier than previous generations.

Generation Z adults (those born between 1997 and 2008) have the lowest savings-to-spending ratio of any generation, according to a Bank of America report. Young adults without a college degree face the highest unemployment rate of any group of workers, at 7.2%. The unemployment rate for young adults with a college degree has also risen, from 4.2% three years ago to 5.7% in June, with many recent graduates struggling in the labor market.

Yet many Gen Zers have kept spending on small indulgences—makeup, coffee—even as inflation and unemployment have climbed.

"For Gen Z, this trend is consistent with the 'little treat economy,' where smaller discretionary indulgences remain appealing and might even be worth spending more on when larger financial milestones feel harder to reach," Bank of America's researchers said.

Why This Matters

Even as they're often putting off buying a home and raising children, Gen Zers are investing earlier than previous generations did. Starting young gives their money more time to compound, which means more wealth by the time they need it.

Gen Zers entered adulthood as the cost of many monthly expenses rose faster than wages, making it harder to reach the middle class.

Home prices have risen about 210% since 2000, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency's house price index. Raising children has grown more costly, as childcare and school costs have climbed nearly 190% since 2000. Meanwhile, wages have grown by only about 84% over the same period.

More than three in 10 Gen Zers say money problems have pushed back their plans to buy a home, and a quarter say the same about having children, according to Northwestern Mutual's 2026 Planning & Progress survey.

While fewer young Americans are buying homes and more of them rely on help from their families to afford a down payment, Gen Zers are ahead of previous generations in investing.

In 2024, 37% of 25-year-olds had moved significant money from checking into an investment account since turning 22, according to the JPMorganChase Institute. In 2015, just 6% had.

Gen Z's higher participation in the stock market results in part from the pandemic-era savings boom, which left young adults with more cash to invest, and a stock market that has more than tripled over the past decade. And as housing has become less affordable, more Gen Zers may be steering their savings into stocks rather than real estate.

Gen Z is also investing in their retirement at higher rates than any generation before them. In a recent survey by Bank of America, the average Gen Z worker started saving for retirement at 24, a decade younger than the average baby boomer.

With Social Security's trust fund projected to run short in the mid-2030s, many Gen Zers are planning to live more off their 401(k)s and IRAs than previous generations. Just 5% of Gen Zers expect Social Security to be their main source of retirement income, according to a 2025 survey by the research firm Cerulli Associates. Among millennials, the generation just ahead of them, 16% do.

"Buy tech bond 'diamonds-in-rough' as AI hyperscalers up equity issuance, cut buybacks," Michael Hartnett, chief investment strategist at Bank of America, said in his latest Flow Show note.

The call comes after a punishing year for tech credit.

Why Hartnett Calls Tech Bonds 'Diamonds in the Rough'

According to Hartnett, U.S. technology bonds have lost about 9% so far in 2026.

That leaves their total return relative to the broad investment-grade bond index at the lowest level in 30 years. In other words, tech debt has rarely looked this cheap compared with the rest of the high-grade market.

title: What the Big Banks' Third-Quarter Reports Say About Credit Card Borrowers
detail:
What the Big Banks' Third-Quarter Reports Say About Credit Card Borrowers
Reuben Gregg Brewer, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 6:35 AM MST 5 min read
MA
BAC
JPM
C
COF
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Credit cards are a huge benefit and a huge risk because they make it easy to spend. And since you don't have to pay the bill for 30 days or so, the hit can sometimes take consumers by surprise. This is why you can get an important read on consumers by looking at the credit card businesses of large banks like Bank of America (NYSE: BAC), JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), Citigroup (NYSE: C), and Capital One (NYSE: COF). The read after the third quarter: the consumer is looking good. Here's the proof.

Banks take on the credit risk

While credit cards usually carry the logos of companies like Visa (NYSE: V) or Mastercard (NYSE: MA), those companies are just payment processors. They charge small fees for facilitating financial transactions; the banks that issue the credit cards bear the financial risk. If a customer doesn't pay their credit card bill, banks like Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, and Capital One have to eat the cost.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

That said, issuing credit cards can be a very profitable business. So there's a balance that has to be struck between risk and reward. And when it comes to the risk side, banks tell you each quarter what's going on. They do this by reporting their 30-day and 90-day delinquency ratios and charge-off ratios. You just have to dig into the financial releases to find the data.

Everything is OK for now

Citigroup's credit card operations had a 30-day delinquency ratio of 1.16% in its own branded card portfolio in the third quarter. In cards it issues for other companies, often called private-label cards, that ratio was 1.96%. Private-label cards tend to be issued to riskier customers. Still, neither figure is particularly bad, and both are lower than they were a year ago. That same story holds for the 90-day delinquency ratios, which came in at 1.21% for Citigroup's cards and 1.92% for private-label cards.

JPMorgan Chase is the same exact story. The fairly strong 1.97% 30-day delinquency rate was down from a year ago. And the even stronger 90-day delinquency rate of 0.96% was also down from a year ago.

Bank of America's story is no different. Its 30-day delinquency rate stood at 2.32% in the third quarter of 2026, down from the same quarter in 2025. Its 90-day delinquency rate was 1.13%, also down year over year. That said, the company also reports net charge-offs, which came in at 3.22%. Like the delinquency rates, the financial giant's charge-offs were lower than they were a year ago.

Capital One tends to take on lower-credit-quality customers. That's probably why its 3.72% 30-day delinquency rate is higher than the other banks here. However, like the other banks, Capital One's 30-day delinquency rate was lower in the third quarter than it was a year ago. That said, it did tick up slightly from the second quarter's 3.37%. It wasn't the only bank to see a sequential increase from the second quarter, but the jump was easily the biggest here. Still, charge-offs fell sequentially and year-over-year to 4.01%, so it doesn't look like the bank's credit risks are getting out of hand.

It looks like consumers are holding up well

The news is filled with stories about the financial strains that consumers are facing. High inflation may be a pain, as costs increase, but increasingly budget-conscious consumers don't appear to have overextended themselves. At least, that's what the credit card data from some of the world's largest financial companies and credit card issuers suggests.

DoorDash (DASH): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2028 (TIKR)

The quarter's beat should help the 2026 and 2027 estimates hold up. The 2028 estimate is harder to call, since DoorDash plans to reinvest more than all of the Instacart synergies in the first year after closing.

At [$179], DoorDash trades at 25x forward earnings, its lowest in five years. Post's $257 works out to 35x expected earnings over the next twelve months. That's above the stock's one-year average of 33x and below its three-year average of 39x.
